title: Maybe AI hate gone too far or just misconception?
author: GaussRausch
selftext:
Ok I was going to post about my project, but now I am posting about what happened when I posted about it

  
Long story short, I am porting a 2000s game called Vampire the masquerade Bloodlines to Unreal

  
It's a behemoth task and I am exploring AI for that, I got to the point no other projects that tried it reached after 20 years! and I posted to the reddit community the game has.

replies.body: Hey man could you share your post mortem history? What hit you? What was your challenges you couldn’t overcome? Is that code laying around somewhere?

replies.author: DaedalusRaistlin
replies.body:
Sure. The main problem was that I had to write a ton of entities that didn't exist in the then current version of Source. Bloodlines was on a much older version, and though I got some scripting working by automatically converting map entity formats (the Ocean House Hotel was pretty spooky!) there was just so much code I had to write myself from scratch.

I'd done some tutorials on the C++ side of Source engine modding, even released some tutorials (VGUI HTML Screens), but the scope of what I had to write to get Bloodlines working on the Source engine properly was just too much. So many GUIs and custom entities to try to figure out. Character models never worked properly, only scenery models. I just couldn't get it working as well as I'd initially hoped.

Someone gave a brief spark of hope when they joined our forums and showed a version of the map compiler that produced working maps for the Bloodlines version of Source. That would have been perfect - we'd simply have to run the custom vbsp.exe and be able to make entire maps for the original engine. But the guy showed some progress screenshots, and then disappeared never to be heard from again. 

These days I'd go down that route - Claude was able to decompile maps from a HL2 mod I worked on in 2007 (Master Blasters). I could probably get it to compile maps too with a medium amount of work - all the map compile tools sources are provided when you make a HL2 mod, so it's easy to reference. The tricky part, which Claude could do for me, is to try to piece together the changes and try to produce something that gives similar results.

replies.author: GaussRausch
replies.body:
This is something I contemplated deciding if I should go unreal or source. One of the reasons that I reasoned is while source being soo similar it would drive me into pinpointing the difference, thing would kinda work but not.  
Character models omg gave me headaches, but I think I landed gave me rough times until I decided to do a binary comparison of how I was solving in memory vs how retail was solving.  
Injected a Frida to watch how the animation grid was solving at runtime and did a database over it then threw Claude to go and start comparing

replies.author: imnotabot303

Smartphones allow anyone access to the internet and social media 24/7 from almost anywhere.

Believe it or not social media has always existed online. It used to just be bulletin boards and forums. The difference is that you needed some basic computer knowledge and a computer which were often too expensive for a lot of people.

Society just isn't ready for people having instant access to millions of people and the world's misinformation at their fingertips at all times. The internet and social media has enabled the masses to be incredibly easily manipulated, especially around things like politics and social issues.

Modern social media definitely hasn't helped but it's the easy access to it that has done the most damage imo.

replies.author: oratualblink

There was also a lot of discussion about radiation, privacy, and, above all, plenty of people saying they would never walk around carrying “a brick.” Today we look back on that period as the early adoption phase, but at the time there was a great deal of criticism and mockery directed at people who owned one, and it was far from obvious that mobile phones would become a technology adopted by the general public. They were often talked about primarily as tools for businesses and professionals.

replies.author: imnotabot303

I didn't like using it in public at all because it instantly drew everyone's attention. You're correct that everyone thought it was for yuppies, either that or drug dealers.

I worked in a mobile store for about a decade over the period from that to everyone having a phone. Nobody really said they wouldn't use one, they were just too expensive and seen as unnecessary for most people at the time. As soon as they became cheaper everyone got one. It wasn't some anti tech thing, it was mainly just cost.

People are actually more anti smartphone now than anyone was about mobile phones back then.

comments.author: BlueAndYellowTowels
comments.body:
I use AI every day at work. I also use it for personal projects. I'm a fan. It's why I'm here.

People are allowed to not like things. Just that simple. I do think people saying "it will pass" are incorrect. AI is directly targeting the livelihoods of millions of people. That's as direct and personal as it gets. Do NOT expect it to get better. Especially, if AI delivers on what it promises to deliver. A lot of good people are going to be struggling and that will reverberate throughout society and will absolutely create a lot of very deep AI resentment, justifiably.

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body:
There's a lot of trolls online that just use anti AI to troll people but there's also a lot of anti AI people that have legitimate concerns about AI. People in AI subs often do the exact thing they are complaining about by lumping everyone that is against certain AI use in with all the trolls and people that just jump on hate bandwagons.

I think AI is an amazing tool but I also think our society just isn't ready for what's coming if AI gets to the level experts are expecting. 

In the creative space content and media is essentially going to become worthless, at least in the indie space. Plus millions of people are going to lose jobs in a lot of industries over the coming decades and governments have nothing in sight to deal with it. Most refuse to even consider things like a basic income for everyone. 

It often feels like everyone in AI subs are living in a rose tinted fantasy where AI is going to usher in some kind of utopia where everyone gets to be creative and make art and get paid for it. AI is potentially going to cause a huge amount of problems in all parts of industry and society. 

It's highly likely the only people making money will be the companies providing AI services. There's a reason AI companies are funneling so much money into it and it is so everyone gets to make a living from making art.

replies.author: BlueAndYellowTowels
replies.body:
I do with governments took a more proactive role in preparing for mass unemployment. That said, if we had something like UBI, for example. Things like this sub or any sub that focusing on creating things and AI can be implicated, would definitely have a shift in tone.

Things are too precarious right now for too many people for them to find any sympathy for a yet another machine replacing them... which is a shame. 

Because I do think AI can create Art. Like, authentically. 

Recently, I wanted to make a 4x game and I walked the AI through a mechanic that was completely new to the genre and I helped it tweak the usability of it and I play tested it and it felt... amazing. It felt completely different from anything I've played in a 4x game. I was super please.

I'm likely going to use that prototype as a baseline for a game I'm about to get into developing.

...and the cool thing is, grand strategy 4x games, they're not made by solo developers. They're rare in the indie space. But with AI, I can now actually implement a vision of a 4x game I've been wanting to make for years.

AI is primed to really change things. But we need to address the "costs" of such a tool.

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body:
Well AI is just a tool and artists will use it that way but many people using AI just want an end result with as little time and effort as possible. 

As AI improves we will get to a point where anyone will be able to create games and just about any other content, by simply asking for it. At that point AI is doing 99% of the creating. Essentially AI content factories.

These AI models will need to be vastly more powerful than what any normal person could run locally which means everyone will be using the AI services of big tech companies. We already see that in this sub, almost nobody is using free open source or local tools, they are all paying subscriptions to big tech. Whilst a few people might be making some money from selling a game most people won't and it's only going to become less and less over time.

It's basically big tech selling the shovels in a gold rush. 

It's all fun and games if it's just a hobby but we're basically giving away the ability for anyone to make money from art and creativity and handing it over to big tech companies. People think AI is empowering indies which it might be at this specific moment in time but almost nobody involved with AI subs is thinking about where it's all going to end up. 

Democratization and hyper-commoditization of the creative industry is not going to end well for anyone but large AI companies.

comments.author: LocoMod
comments.body:
Don't post the progress for something like this. Post the result. And only if its better than the original. A lot of things with AI are easy when you are starting out, then they get abandoned because the user hits a wall that their experience can't overcome even with AI tools. This is what slop ultimately is. Showing off the low effort progress. 99% of those projects die a few days after they are posted and it wastes everyones time.

If you're going to use AI and showcase your project made with it, you need to show something mind blowing for the estimated level of effort the audience will judge you on.

If the audience didnt push back on this, there would be a flood of trash that would take over everything.

I love AI. I think its the most powerful tool ever made. I despise low effort slop. Whether AI was used or not.

comments.author: ImpossibleImpact1
comments.body:
I remember when I started DJ'ing 14 years ago. My first purchase was a digital controller - much cheaper, and in some regards superior to the CDJ's and vinyl players that existed back then.

However, it made the art of transitioning from one song to another much easier to learn and grasp. Purists said it's the deteriorisation of the hobby's art.

Fast forward 14 years, and all club players have taken ahold of the controller advantages - and much more. It's still 'cool' to play analog or with old school, harder-to-beatmatch material, but the fact is that the crowd simply will generally have a better time if the DJ has access to the newest technology.

Make of that analogy what you will!

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body:
Theres nuance to that though. I used to DJ back in the 90s using 1210s and vinyl. It took a lot more manual skill and planning than using digital based hardware and music. Digital taking over allowed people to do a lot more because things like beach matching because became far easier. 

So if someone then uses that tech advancement to perform even better sets then that's great. However the majority just do the same thing or less than turntable DJs were doing only now they need less skill to do it. Plus that massively increased the amount of DJs and competition. We basically ended up with a lot of "DJ slop" where people are just stood in front of the equipment doing almost nothing but pretending to tweak a few knobs now and again.

replies.author: ImpossibleImpact1
replies.body:
You're absolutely right about that. Many controller DJ's are simply not very good, but they would be even worse on regular decks. And I think it translates to AI usage quite well!

Experts in a field will almost certainly get better use out of AI implementation than newbies, because they can feel where it lightens their workload and where it struggles!

That said I just hired a guy with a digital setup for my wedding and he was outstanding.

replies.author: imnotabot303
replies.body:
Yes, I always find it funny to watch some of these new DJs, everything has become so easy they don't know what to do with themselves so they just end up spending half the time dancing and pretending to tweak knobs in between tracks.

There's always going to be talented people who can take advantage of tech advancements. I have seen some really good DJs taking things to a whole new level. This is 10 years old now and a DMC set but it shows some of the technical stuff talented people can do with just some tech advancements.

https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=44F0d2CbjM0&pp=ygUhZGogYnJhY2UgLSAyMDE2IGRtYyBvbmxpbmUgZmluYWxz

The main issue though is that the easier something becomes the more people there are doing it and the harder it is to get noticed. It also brings down the value of that thing because there's so much competition.

AI is something different though, it's gradually reducing the bar to zero. It won't be long before your granny can ask AI to generate a game. At that point the value of those AI generated things also becomes zero.

Unfortunately there's a lot of people online that do lie and do steal work etc so that makes some people paranoid. It won't ever end and it will only get worse as AI gets better. In a decade or so nobody will care because 99% of the content online will be made with AI unfortunately.

When we inevitably get to the stage where we can fold space to close the distance between two points and bypass the factor of light speed, one person will die by a freak accident and everyone is going to say that it's some awful thing no one should ever use and eventually no one will care and use it in their every day life.
